When your nervous system starts firing on all cylinders, taking the edge off with a quick fix—say, an edible, a stiff drink, or something from the medicine cabinet—might sound appealing. But before you clock out with chemicals, know that there are other ways to bring yourself back down to earth that are completely natural and yield real relief. We’ve rounded up some of the most effective options for how to reduce stress naturally below—none of which lean on substances or require you to become a Zen master overnight.
How to Reduce Stress Naturally
1. Take a breath

Stress can lead to tightness in the chest, shallow breathing, and tension in the neck or shoulders, says Marissa Honjiyo, LMFT, a therapist in Santa Ana, California. Sound like familiar territory? If so, she suggests taking a beat and doing a few breathing exercises. Popular options include box breathing (which involves inhaling, holding, exhaling, and holding for four seconds each) and 4-7-8 breathing (inhaling for four seconds, holding for seven seconds, and exhaling for eight seconds). Prefer something more casual? Ditch the counting and simply slow your breathing down.

Breathwork can even soften physical tension. “When your chest and jaw are holding something, a long exhale is what discharges it,” says Rod Mitchell, MSc, MC, a registered psychologist and the clinical director at Emotions Therapy Calgary. This one’s a swift solution when you need to settle down fast—like outside your boss’s office or before giving a speech at your buddy’s wedding. Ditto for rolling your shoulders.
2. Move your body

blocks.x: When stress puts you in a chokehold, give all that nervous energy somewhere to go. “Exercise is one of the most reliable ways to regulate stress because stress prepares the body for action, and we need to dump that cortisol somewhere,” says Matthew Leahy, PhD, a clinical psychologist in Dallas, Texas. The next time you’re under pressure, get up and lift heavy, take a HIIT class, or hop on the treadmill. “Getting your heart rate up and working up a sweat can be a great way to improve mood, release endorphins, and get your mind off of the stress,” says Honjiyo.
But you don’t necessarily have to go balls to the wall to feel better. Even a 10-minute brisk walk has been shown to improve mood.
3. Refer to yourself in the third person

Strange and slightly weird, but surprisingly legit: dropping the first person and talking to yourself by your name can help you create some distance between you and your stressor. “It sounds a little silly, but research backs it up,” Mitchell says. “People tend to think more clearly about a problem when it is not grammatically theirs.” While you’re at it, distance yourself from your narrative and aim to be more objective. For instance, instead of saying “I’m going to bomb this first date,” say, “Joe’s nervous, but Joe’s survived worse than an awkward Hinge date.”
4. Meditate
Naturally, meditation is on this list. Even if the thought of it makes you squirm or roll your eyes, know that there’s a reason why every therapist and self-help guru recommends it.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 17 randomized trials found that mindfulness-based interventions (including meditation) meaningfully reduced perceived stress in otherwise healthy adults. Some research also suggests that mindfulness and meditation may influence cortisol, a key hormone involved in the stress response.

blocks.x: Fortunately, you don’t need to hold a lotus position for an hour to reap the benefits. Even brief bouts have been shown to curb stress, so starting with five or 10 minutes can be better than doing nothing at all. Need some hand-holding, or can’t bear pin-drop silence? Stream a guided meditation to let someone lead you through it. While a single session could leave you feeling calmer and clearer, just note that a consistent practice yields the best results. On the flipside, a recent Atlantic story found that especially intensive meditation can sometimes be disruptive to sleep or have other negative psychological effects—so take note of how it makes you feel before you go all in.
5. Put on something calming

There’s classical music. Sounds of raindrops. Binaural beats. Heck, even sound baths if you’re open to a little woo-woo in your life. Research suggests that different music- and sound-based interventions have the potential to reduce stress; it’s just a matter of choosing which one works for you. Test the waters by putting on an ambient playlist on Spotify. Or, experiment with apps that offer a range of soundscapes (GQ’s Wellness & Grooming director is a fan of Soaak).
6. Head outdoors

You don’t need to disappear into a national park every time your cortisol spikes. But most of us would benefit by leaning on Mother Nature when we’re caught in a stress spiral. “Nature gives the brain a break from the constant demands on attention that come with work, traffic, and constant digital use,” Leahy says. Even if you live in a major city and the nearest forest or beach is hours away, make an effort to head to a nearby park—or even the closest tree-lined street—the next time anxiety hits. “Even relatively brief exposure to green or blue spaces can help people feel less mentally overloaded,” says Leahy.
7. Dabble in hobbies

blocks.x: News flash: not everything you do needs to optimize your health, advance your career, or become a side hustle. Sometimes—especially when you’re stressed—you should do something just because you enjoy it.

So pick up a guitar, play basketball, or test out an elaborate new recipe. Any number of hobbies can help you relax and create distance between you and your stressor—not to mention add some pleasure into your life. “Hobbies work as long as you don’t know how to perform them on auto-pilot,” Mitchell says. He suggests going beyond bingeing Netflix and scrolling on your phone. Instead, aim for activities that keep you active and engaged, not merely stimulated or distracted.
8. Hang out with someone

Sometimes the last thing your stressed-out brain needs is more alone time with itself. All three experts agree that spending time with others is one of the most effective ways to lower stress naturally. “Simply sitting near someone calm can help regulate your own nervous system without having to talk through your issues together. That’s what we call co-regulation,” Mitchell says. Spending time with other people also gives you a reprieve to get out of your head and interrupt the constant mental loop. And if you do decide to unload, they may be able to see an obvious solution that you’re blind to when you’re in the weeds.
9. Protect your sleep

Stress and anxiety can leave you restless at night, but it’s important to do what you can to protect your shuteye. “Sleep is both a stress intervention and a stress-prevention strategy,” Leahy says. “When people are sleep deprived, the brain becomes more reactive and everyday frustrations can feel much larger than they otherwise would.” That makes staying up until 1 a.m. trying to solve tomorrow’s problem a crappy bargain: You’re sacrificing one of the things that could make you better equipped to deal with the issue at hand.

So give yourself a cutoff time for problem-solving, and make it a point to set the stage for a good night’s rest. To avoid tossing and turning, try sleep-friendly interventions like unwinding with a warm bath, reading instead of scrolling, or brewing lemon balm tea.
